item.title: ‘President has restored our national pride and self-belief’
item.description: Debra Matabvu PRESIDENT Mnangagwa has made Zimbabweans believe in their ability to build their country using local resources and capabilities, while drawing inspiration from the country’s rich and inspirational heritage, Deputy Chief Secretary in the Office of the President and Cabinet (Presidential Communications) Mr George Charamba has said. In an interview on the eve of President Mnangagwa’s 84th birthday last week, Mr Charamba reflected on the President’s leadership since 2017, describing him as a leader who has helped rebuild national confidence after years of economic challenges and political upheaval. Zimbabwe’s weakened sense of confidence, he said, should be understood against the backdrop of the country’s difficult post-independence history, including hardships occasioned by the Economic Structural Adjustment Programme (ESAP) and sanctions imposed following the Land Reform Programme, among other challenges. These successive challenges, Mr Charamba said, placed significant strain on the country and its people, making the restoration of national confidence and pride an important part of the country’s development journey. “In comes ED (President Mnangagwa) in 2017, he is presiding over a nation whose spirit is battered, really battered,” said Mr Charamba. “A sense of diminished self-worth and he has to rehabilitate; he has to reconstruct that spirit, nurture it in such a way that he ends up presiding over the people who are aware of self-belief. I think, for me, that did it. He restored our mojo, if you want. Wherever you see us, you see the people who walk with that strength of self-belief in us.” ‘A country is built by its own people’ Mr Charamba said President Mnangagwa’s call to action, which is delivered through his mantra “Nyika inovakwa nevene vayo/Ilizwe lakhiwa ngabanikazi balo” (A country is built by its people), has its origins in the liberation struggle. He said the philosophy had been supported by deliberate interventions aimed at building domestic productive capacity, restoring self-belief and reducing reliance on external solutions. Education 5.0, he added, was one such intervention that transformed the emphasis of local education beyond knowledge consumption towards problem-solving, innovation and production. “I think there is a way of looking at Education 5.0 as part of the President’s belief in the people he guides,” he said. “So, when you are creating those incubators at a tertiary level, what you are saying is you are summoning the national intellect, canalising it towards nation-building, which means it is actually building on this self-belief that I was talking about.” A inspirational legacy Mr Charamba said the concept of Education 5.0 had also seen the country moving towards increased production of locally made goods. “If you take us from 1982 to 2016, all that period we were overly political as a State. What the President brought in post-2017 was a State which was literate in terms of the marketplace. “Now when you link it with Education 5.0, you realise there is a sense of seamless continuity. You prime the intellect, you translate that intellect into production, you grow the economy to a point where just now, we average something like 5,3 percent per annum growth, completely unheard of in this country.” The construction of major infrastructure such as roads and dams, Mr Charamba said, was not only about facilitating economic activity. He said the projects also demonstrated Zimbabweans’ capacity to take charge of their own development, thereby strengthening the sense of self-belief he identified as a key feature of the President’s leadership. This approach, he said, was consistent with the broader emphasis on using local capabilities to drive national development. Mr Charamba also linked the restoration of national confidence to the introduction of Munhumutapa Day, saying the commemoration was intended to draw inspiration from the country’s history rather than establish any form of monarchy. He said Great Zimbabwe, which is associated with the Munhumutapa civilisation, represented resilience, creativity and the ability of Zimbabwe’s ancestors to build structures that have endured for centuries. “There are lots of empty debates around his declaring Munhumutapa Day and people symbolically saying he (the President) is trying to create a kingdom out of a constitutional democracy,” he said. “Great nations are built on a great past. You envision, you imagine your futures; your national strength on the basis of the history that has been bequeathed to you by your own people. “You notice at some point the kingdom of Munhumutapa actually shared borders with Abyssinia, present-day Ethiopia, “That’s how expansive Zimbabwe was in history. That’s how expansive Zimbabwe is in present times. “So, really what the President is doing is to give back our sense of self-belief, our sense of strength which history gave us.” Mr Charamba said the historical legacy represented by Munhumutapa and Great Zimbabwe could provide the people with a stronger sense of identity and confidence as the country pursued development. He also described President Mnangagwa as a family man who is down to earth and strongly abhors corruption. President Mnangagwa celebrated his 84th birthday on September 15, which coincided with Munhumutapa Day. (via Sundaymail) #Zimbabwe #ZimbabweNews

item.title: Traceable question papers, personalised answer sheets for this year’s exams
item.description: Ivan Zhakata LEARNERS sitting for this year’s Zimbabwe School Examinations Council public examinations will use personalised answer sheets and question papers that are traceable as part of new enhanced security measures. The new features, which are designed to prevent cheating and safeguard the integrity of local exams, make it possible to trace question papers to centres to which they were allocated, while personalised answer sheets are designed to prevent the substitution or smuggling of scripts into examination rooms. The measures cover the entire examination chain, from the printing and packaging of question papers to their distribution, storage and eventual use by candidates. The enhanced security measures come as Grade Seven examinations begin tomorrow, while Ordinary and Advanced Level examinations will start on October 12. Zimsec public relations manager Mrs Nicky Dhlamini said the council was fully prepared for the exams. “The season for final examinations is upon us, starting with the Grade Seven examinations on the 21st of September 2026,” she said. “Zimsec is fully prepared for the start of the examinations. Question papers and stationery are already being distributed to the cluster centres ready for collection by centres.” Security and examination integrity, Mrs Dhlamini said, remained a priority, with technological advances in the printing and packaging of examination materials strengthening the safeguards. She said security features embedded in examination materials enable Zimsec to identify the centre to which particular question papers had been allocated. “From printing to distribution and eventually the sitting of examinations, everything is closely monitored by security and loss-control teams,” she said. The tracking system means should candidates gain premature access to question papers, security teams can track the materials to their centre of origin, allowing investigations to focus on the source of the breach. The measures were designed to ensure that investigations targeted those responsible without prejudicing innocent candidates. “In close collaboration with State and private agencies, Zimsec is able to identify and punish only the guilty without prejudicing innocent candidates,” she said. Zimsec has also strengthened safeguards against the use of unauthorised scripts during examinations through the personalisation of answer sheets. Mrs Dhlamini said the measure would help prevent malpractice involving the substitution or introduction of scripts from outside the examination room. “Personalisation of answer sheets also prevents malpractice involving foreign scripts being smuggled from outside the examination room,” she said. The measures are part of broader efforts to protect the credibility of the national examination system and ensure that candidates are assessed fairly. A total of 800 003 candidates are expected to sit the November 2026 examinations. Of these, 345 368 are O-Level candidates, 40 843 are at A-Level, while 413 792 are Grade Seven candidates. The examinations will be written at 2 616 O-Level centres, 925 A-Level centres and 5 646 Grade Seven centres. The scale of the examinations requires close coordination between Zimsec, schools, security agencies and other stakeholders to ensure the secure movement, storage and handling of examination materials. Mrs Dhlamini encouraged the public to report suspected malpractice and maladministration. “We urge you to report through our Axcentium tip-offs anonymous platform or to your nearest Zimsec office,” she said. (via Sundaymail) #Zimbabwe #ZimbabweNews

item.title: WATCH: Scores gather for prisons golf tournament
item.description: Lovemore Dube SCORES of golfers, including inmates from Bulawayo and Khami prison, gathered at Harry Allen Golf Club in Bulawayo on Saturday for the Commissioner-General’s Goodwill Trust Fund Golf Tournament. [caption id=attachment_5572273 align=alignnone width=1024] King Fisher, a six year old is among the participants at the Prisons and Correctional Services Golf Tournament at Harry Allen Golf Club on Saturday[/caption] Golfers from across Zimbabwe took part in the tournament, with various provinces of the Zimbabwe Prisons and Correctional Services (ZPCS) sending teams to the event. [caption id=attachment_5572303 align=alignnone width=1024] Norman Sibanda an inmate gets a feel of real tournament golf on the fairway after teeing of at Hole 15 at Harry Allen Golf Club on Saturday at the Zimbabwe Prison and Correctional Services Commissioner General Fundraising Golf Tournament[/caption] The tournament is the second edition since its launch and, for the first time, inmates are participating alongside members of the public. [caption id=attachment_5572318 align=alignnone width=1024] Inmates among those to tee off[/caption] Colleges and universities from Bulawayo are also taking part in the event, which is being held under the theme: “Rekindling Hope Through — Teeing Up Second Chances.” [embed]https://youtu.be/8gQUegZfP5I[/embed] Funds raised from the tournament will be used to support orphaned children of former ZPCS members, as well as other vulnerable children from the general public. [embed]https://youtu.be/n24mRakY_5M[/embed] [caption id=attachment_5572313 align=alignnone width=1024] City businessman Jabulani Nkomo officially tees of to mark the start of the Zimbabwe Prison and Correctional Services Golf Tournament at Harry Allen Golf Club on Saturday[/caption] City businessman Jabulani Nkomo performed the official tee-off alongside Bulawayo Metropolitan Provincial chief Mkhulunyelwa Ngwenya. (via The Sunday News) #Zimbabwe #ZimbabweNews
item.dc:creator: The Sunday News
